title: Stone, Bronze, Iron
description: The first technologies — and how they reshaped human society

concepts.title: Stone-Age Tools
concepts.contentHtml:
The earliest known stone tools — Lomekwian, found in Kenya — date to roughly 3.3 million years ago, predating our own genus Homo. By 2.6 million years ago, sharp-edged Oldowan flakes were widespread across East Africa. Around 1.7 million years ago the more refined Acheulean hand-axe appeared and remained essentially unchanged for over a million years — the longest-running technological tradition in human history.

Two later innovations transformed daily life:

  • Controlled fire — at least 1 million years ago, definitively by 400,000 years ago. Fire enabled cooking (which substantially boosted nutrient availability and possibly enabled larger brains), warmth, light, and protection.
  • Composite tools and the bow — modern humans developed tools combining multiple materials: spear-throwers (atlatls) by ~30,000 years ago, the bow and arrow by perhaps 70,000 years ago in Africa.

The wheel, often imagined as ancient and ubiquitous, was a relative late-comer — the earliest known wheeled vehicles date to about 3500 BCE in Mesopotamia, well after agriculture, pottery, and metallurgy.

concepts.title: Agriculture and the Settled Life
concepts.contentHtml:
The single most consequential technological transition in human history was the Neolithic Revolution — the shift from foraging to settled agriculture, which began independently in at least seven world regions:

  • The Fertile Crescent (~10,000 BCE) — wheat, barley, lentils, sheep, goats.
  • China — millet (north) and rice (south), pigs.
  • Mesoamerica — maize, beans, squash.
  • The Andes — potatoes, quinoa, llamas.
  • New Guinea, Sub-Saharan Africa, and eastern North America also saw independent domestications.

Settled life made possible long-term storage, division of labour, larger populations, and eventually cities. It also brought new problems: zoonotic disease (smallpox, measles, influenza), shorter average stature than foragers, and new forms of inequality. Pottery, weaving, brewing, and irrigation followed within a few thousand years.

concepts.title: The Bronze and Iron Ages
concepts.contentHtml:
The smelting of metal opened new possibilities:

  • Copper — worked in cold form by 8000 BCE, smelted by ~5000 BCE.
  • Bronze (copper + ~10 % tin) — emerged around 3300 BCE in West Asia. Harder than copper alone and able to take a sharp edge, bronze gave armies new weapons (swords, shields, helmets) and craftsmen new tools. Tin's geographic rarity drove long-distance trade — Cornish tin reached the Mediterranean.
  • Iron — initial use of meteoritic iron in Egypt; large-scale smelting of iron from ore began around 1200 BCE in Anatolia (the Hittites). Iron was harder to work but the ore was abundant. The collapse of the Bronze Age civilisations around 1200 BCE accelerated iron's adoption.

By 500 BCE, iron tools and weapons had spread across Eurasia. Cheap, hard cutting edges meant deeper ploughs, denser populations, and larger armies. The technology underwrote the rise of classical civilisations from Han China to the Roman Republic.

title: Information Technology
description: Writing, paper, printing, and the telegraph — moving information across space and time

concepts.title: Writing
concepts.contentHtml:
Writing was invented independently at least three times:

  • Cuneiform in Sumer, c. 3200 BCE — pictographs evolving into wedge-shaped marks impressed on clay tablets.
  • Egyptian hieroglyphs, c. 3200 BCE — possibly influenced by Mesopotamian models.
  • Chinese oracle-bone script, c. 1200 BCE — the direct ancestor of modern Chinese characters.
  • Mesoamerican scripts (Olmec/Maya), c. 1000–500 BCE — independently developed.

The most consequential downstream invention was the alphabet: the Phoenicians (c. 1050 BCE) reduced Egyptian-derived signs to about 22 consonant letters. The Greeks added vowels around 800 BCE; from Greek descend Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic, Hebrew, and most other major alphabets.

Once writing existed, ledgers, laws, contracts, religious texts, and lasting historical records became possible. Civilisations without writing left huge archaeological imprints but limited textual ones. The pre-Columbian quipu of the Inca — knotted cords — was a sophisticated record-keeping system that may or may not count as 'writing', depending on the definition.

concepts.title: Paper, Printing, and Mass Literacy
concepts.contentHtml:
The materials of writing matter as much as writing itself:

  • Papyrus (Egypt, ~3000 BCE) — the oldest writing surface, made from reeds.
  • Parchment (Pergamon, ~200 BCE) — animal skin, durable but expensive.
  • Paper — invented in China by Cai Lun around 105 CE; transmitted via the Islamic world to Europe by the 13th century.
  • Movable type — first developed in Song China by Bi Sheng in 1040 (using ceramic type) but limited by Chinese script's huge character set.
  • Gutenberg's press (c. 1450) — combined movable metal type with the screw press and oil-based ink. Within 50 years, an estimated 20 million books had been printed in Europe.

Printing's effects were transformative: literacy rates climbed; scientific knowledge could circulate quickly and accurately; the Reformation depended on Bibles and pamphlets in vernacular languages. The Encyclopédie, the rise of newspapers, and the Enlightenment public sphere all depended on the underlying printing technology.

concepts.title: The Telegraph and Beyond
concepts.contentHtml:
For most of history, information moved no faster than the fastest horse, ship, or pigeon. The 19th century broke that limit.

  • Optical semaphore (Chappe, France, 1792) — the first long-distance signalling network, but limited by line-of-sight and weather.
  • Electric telegraph (Cooke and Wheatstone in Britain; Morse in the US, both 1830s–40s) — sent messages along wires at the speed of electricity. Morse code (1844) became the global standard.
  • Transatlantic cable (1858; reliable from 1866) — reduced messages between London and New York from weeks to minutes.
  • Telephone (Bell, 1876) — voice rather than coded messages.
  • Radio (Marconi, 1895; first transatlantic transmission 1901) — wireless, point-to-multipoint.

By 1900, instantaneous global communication was a reality for those who could afford it. The 20th century would extend this with broadcast radio, television, satellites, fibre optics, and the internet — each step continuing the trend of more information moving faster between more people for less cost.

title: Steam, Electricity, and the Industrial World
description: How energy technologies remade the world from 1700 to 1900

concepts.title: Steam Power
concepts.contentHtml:
For most of human history, useful work came from human muscle, animals, water wheels, and windmills — collectively limited to perhaps 1 kW per worker. The steam engine shattered this constraint.

  • Newcomen's atmospheric engine (1712) was the first commercially successful steam engine, used to pump water out of coal mines. Inefficient, but transformative.
  • James Watt's separate condenser (1769) cut fuel use by ~75 %, then his rotary engine (1781) extended steam from pumping to driving any kind of machinery.
  • High-pressure engines from Trevithick (~1800) made steam mobile: locomotives and steamships followed.

Steam transformed manufacturing, transport, and the geography of cities. Stephenson's Rocket (1829) won the Rainhill Trials at 47 km/h; by 1850, Britain had over 10,000 km of railway. Steamships crossed the Atlantic regularly from the 1840s. The Industrial Revolution, the urbanisation of Europe, and the integration of global commodity markets all depended on steam.

concepts.title: Electricity
concepts.contentHtml:
Electricity moved from laboratory curiosity to industrial backbone in just a few decades:

  • Volta's pile (1800) provided the first reliable source of steady current.
  • Faraday demonstrated electromagnetic induction in 1831 — the principle of generators and electric motors.
  • Maxwell's equations (1864) unified electricity, magnetism, and light.
  • Edison's incandescent bulb (1879) and the first electric utility (Pearl Street Station, New York, 1882) brought electric lighting to homes and businesses.
  • Tesla and Westinghouse championed alternating current; the AC system won out for long-distance transmission and was demonstrated dramatically at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair.

By 1900, electric motors, lighting, streetcars, and elevators were reshaping cities. The dynamo had become the second great prime mover after steam, and unlike steam it could be subdivided and sent at the speed of light to any point in a city.

concepts.title: Internal Combustion and the Second Industrial Revolution
concepts.contentHtml:
The decades around 1900 saw a clustering of major technological breakthroughs sometimes called the Second Industrial Revolution:

  • Internal combustion engines (Otto, 1876; Diesel, 1893) — lighter and more flexible than steam.
  • The automobile (Benz's Patent-Motorwagen, 1886; Ford's Model T from 1908) — mass-produced personal transport.
  • Powered flight — the Wright brothers' first sustained flight at Kitty Hawk in December 1903.
  • The Haber-Bosch process (1909) — synthetic ammonia, enabling industrial fertiliser and arguably allowing modern population levels.
  • The Bessemer process (1856) and continuous steel production transformed construction. Steel skyscrapers, bridges, and rails became cheap and ubiquitous.

By the eve of World War I, the everyday material world looked recognisably modern: steel cities, electric light, telephones, motorcars, aeroplanes, mass-produced consumer goods, and chemical industry were all in place. World GDP per capita had roughly doubled since 1800 — and was about to double again over the following century.

title: Electronics and Computing
description: From vacuum tubes to integrated circuits to the personal computer

concepts.title: Vacuum Tubes and the First Computers
concepts.contentHtml:
The vacuum tube (de Forest's triode, 1906) was the first electronic device that could amplify and switch — making radio, television, and electronic computers possible.

The first programmable electronic computers were built during World War II:

  • Colossus (Bletchley Park, 1943) — used to break Lorenz cipher messages between Hitler and his generals. Long classified, only widely known after the 1970s.
  • ENIAC (Pennsylvania, 1945) — 18,000 vacuum tubes; programmed by physically rewiring patch panels; weighed 27 tonnes.
  • Manchester Baby (1948) — first stored-program computer.

These machines validated Alan Turing's 1936 theoretical work on universal computation: any computable function could be performed by a sufficiently powerful general-purpose machine. The shift from special-purpose to general-purpose computing would define the next 80 years.

concepts.title: Transistor, Integrated Circuit, Microprocessor
concepts.contentHtml:
Vacuum tubes were bulky, hot, and unreliable. The transistor, invented at Bell Labs by Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley in December 1947, replaced them with a tiny, cool, solid-state device. It is arguably the most important invention of the 20th century.

The next leap came in 1958–59 when Jack Kilby (Texas Instruments) and Robert Noyce (Fairchild) independently invented the integrated circuit, putting multiple transistors on a single silicon chip. Moore's Law (Gordon Moore, 1965) noticed that the number of transistors per chip was doubling roughly every 18–24 months — a trend that has held, with caveats, for over half a century.

In 1971, Intel released the 4004 — the first commercial microprocessor — with 2,300 transistors. Today's flagship CPUs and GPUs contain tens of billions. The whole edifice of modern digital civilisation — phones, cars, cloud, satellites, AI — rests on this exponential progress.

concepts.title: Personal Computers, the Internet, and Smartphones
concepts.contentHtml:
Three breakthroughs of the 1970s–90s created the consumer computing world:

  • The personal computer — Altair 8800 (1975), Apple II (1977), IBM PC (1981) brought computing into homes and offices.
  • The Internet — the ARPANET went live in 1969; the Internet Protocol Suite (TCP/IP) became the universal language in 1983; the World Wide Web (Tim Berners-Lee, 1989, publicly available 1991) gave it a friendly interface.
  • The smartphone — Nokia and BlackBerry pioneered mobile data, but Apple's iPhone (2007) defined the modern category. By 2020, more than 5 billion people had access to a mobile phone.

Each step roughly multiplied the number of people with access to computing by an order of magnitude. The transition from rooms full of vacuum tubes to a billion smartphones in 80 years is one of the steepest technological trajectories in history — and it is far from over.

title: The Digital Age and Beyond
description: Internet, biotech, AI, and the technologies of the 21st century

concepts.title: The Internet's Cultural Effects
concepts.contentHtml:
The internet's impact has been comparable to that of the printing press — and it happened roughly ten times faster:

  • Email (1971), the Web (1991), mass adoption from the mid-1990s.
  • E-commerce (Amazon 1994, eBay 1995) restructured retail.
  • Search (Google 1998) made the Web's contents navigable.
  • Social media (Facebook 2004, YouTube 2005, Twitter 2006) changed how billions of people relate to news, politics, and each other.
  • Cloud computing (AWS 2006) replaced owned servers with utility-style compute, enabling new business models.
  • Streaming (Netflix 2007 streaming pivot, Spotify 2008) eliminated physical media for film and music.

Each shift has been accompanied by significant social side effects — privacy erosion, attention economies, misinformation, geopolitical contests over data and platforms. The same technological substrate has empowered movements for democracy and authoritarian control alike.

concepts.title: Biotech and Materials Frontiers
concepts.contentHtml:
The 21st century has seen biotechnology take its place alongside electronics as a defining technological frontier:

  • Genome sequencing — the cost of sequencing a human genome fell from ~$3 billion (2003) to ~$200 (2024), faster than Moore's Law.
  • CRISPR-Cas9 (2012) made gene editing precise and routine.
  • mRNA vaccines (developed over decades, deployed globally during COVID-19) are now being applied to flu, RSV, and cancer.
  • Synthetic biology — engineered yeast producing artemisinin or insulin; bacteria engineered to produce plastics or fuels.

Materials science has advanced in parallel: graphene (isolated 2004), engineered metamaterials, perovskite solar cells, lithium-ion batteries reaching $100/kWh and below — bringing electric vehicles to mass market and reshaping the energy system. The most exciting modern technologies often appear at the intersection of disciplines.

concepts.title: Artificial Intelligence
concepts.contentHtml:
Artificial intelligence has gone through several boom-and-bust cycles since Turing's 1950 essay 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence'. The current explosion began with deep learning's breakthroughs:

  • 2012 — AlexNet wins the ImageNet competition, demonstrating deep neural networks' superiority for image recognition.
  • 2016 — DeepMind's AlphaGo defeats the human world champion at Go, a game considered far harder than chess for computers.
  • 2017 — the Transformer architecture introduced; quickly becomes the basis of modern language models.
  • 2020 — AlphaFold solves the 50-year-old protein-folding problem.
  • 2022 onward — ChatGPT and successive large language models bring AI into everyday public use; image generation models follow rapidly.

AI is now reshaping software, science, education, medicine, and warfare in real time. Whether it represents an inflection point comparable to printing, electricity, or the internet — or something even larger — is one of the central open questions of this century. The history of technology suggests that consequences are usually deeper, slower, and stranger than early forecasts predict.
